samples: This program prints a small plain-text statement for two hard-coded sample invoices (ACME and Globex), with one fixed-width row per customer showing the customer name, line count and discounted total, sorted by customer name. After the rows it prints a grand total, which comes to 9.00 for ACME plus 21.00 for Globex, so 30.00. The invoice math (line totals, percentage discount, rounding to cents) lives in the separate invoice module, and the report only needs console output, with no files or network. It is a demo rather than a reusable tool, because the invoices are built into the program and nothing is read from input, though the row-formatting and grand-total functions could be reused with other invoice data.

This program prints a plain-text statement for two hard-coded sample invoices (ACME and Globex). It lists them sorted by customer, one fixed-width row each showing customer name, number of lines and total, then a closing grand total. Each invoice total comes from the reusable `invoice` module: line quantity times unit price, minus a percentage discount, rounded to the cent. The sample data is built into `main`, so you would need to change that code to report on your own invoices, though the row-formatting and grand-total functions can be reused with any list of invoices.

This program prints a fixed-width statement for two hardcoded sample invoices (ACME and Globex), one row per customer in alphabetical order. Each row shows the customer name, the number of lines and the discounted total rounded to cents, and a grand total follows (about 30.00 for the samples). It only writes to the console and takes no input, so as a standalone program it is a demo. Its real value is the two public helpers, one that formats an invoice row and one that sums invoice totals, which build on the separate invoice module's cent-exact, percentage-discount arithmetic.

This program prints a plain-text statement for two hardcoded sample invoices (ACME and Globex). It shows one fixed-width row per invoice, sorted by customer name, with the customer, the number of lines and the discounted total rounded to cents, followed by a grand total of about 30.00. It needs only console output, with no files or network, and the row formatting and grand-total functions are reusable. As shipped, though, it is a demo: it cannot read real invoice data without you replacing the sample invoices.

This program prints a fixed-column statement for two hardcoded sample invoices (ACME and Globex), one row per customer in alphabetical order. Each row shows the customer name, the number of lines and the discounted total, and a grand total follows, which should come to 30.00 (9.00 for ACME plus 21.00 for Globex). It reuses the `invoice` module for the cent-rounded, percentage-discounted totals and needs only console output, so it is a self-contained demo that reads no input and cannot be pointed at your own data without editing it.
